comment.value:
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comments and helpful suggestions!
But based on your written strengths section, we don't know exactly why you gave soundness "fair" and presentation "fair". Can you please elaborate on this? 

# Weaknesses

>"The idea of using cost-to-go differences or relative value was explored earlier in [1], so perhaps the idea of estimating value difference is not necessarily novel. However, its application in DeepRL might be novel."

We thank the reviewer for pointing out [1] and added it to related work. However, we find it challenging to follow the argument. Based on the novelty critique with [1] from 1997, one can argue that all Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) research is not novel since their theory was already "explored" in the 90s. Correct us if we are wrong, but your argument sounds like: "Q-learning was not novel in 2013, and therefore DQN lacks novelty." Although Q-learning predates DQN, DQN is still considered a substantial contribution by the community!

But, please read TLDR and the full answer where we adress your concern (at the end of our entire message).

**TLDR:** Dimitri Bertsekas's short conference paper from 1997 does mention cost-to-go differences (thanks, we now cite it in related work), but it remains a high-level approach with limited development. Bertsekas has the intuition that relative quantities can be beneficial, but he leaves the idea largely unexplored. In any case, we modernized and expanded it substantially.
Theory is always a good start, but the method also needs to work. No experiments are given. No explanation on how to design a good function approximator (antisymmetry is useful) or how to handle episodic environments like Atari (needs four case distinctions for value targets).
No consideration on how to scale this idea up to a problem like Atari (our new trajectory ranking algorithm is very much needed). We strongly emphasize that this idea has not been really explored or robustified in that particular paper or elsewhere. Our paper is substantially novel! And it is the first significant step towards relative value learning that is general applicable, theoretically grounded, modern and scalable!


> The proposed approach does not necessarily improve over the PPO baseline in the evaluated benchmark [...]

Please, see our general comment. 

**TLDR:** By fixing a bug in our code, we now beat the PPO baseline in 61% (47% before) of the games!! We also improve our performance in comparison to DAE (now 75%, previously 61%)! 

>  [... ]it would be good to also indicate the observed variance in scores to suitably contrast against the baselines.

Please, see our general comment. 

**TLDR:** Good point. For statistical significance, we increased the number of seeds to 10 per game and report variance and additional metrics now.

We thank the reviewer for highlighting several strengths of our work and for providing constructive feedback that helped us further improve the paper.

# Weaknesses

> The paper does not beat state-of-the-art results in the experiments

Please, see our general comment.

**TLDR:** We further improved our results by fixing a small bug. Now, our method PPO+RV beats PPO in 61% of the games (before 47%) and DAE in 75% of the games (61% before)!! Also, we added std dev (Table 1) and show additional aggregated metrics (Figure 3).   

> The paper is well written with clear mathematical reasoning but I found some parts a little less straightforward in the explanations (e.g. relative value initialization, see also the question below)

Thank you for the kind words on the paper’s clarity. In general, relative value initialization is applied to improve the credit assignment problem by reducing the influence/effect of $B_t$. We clarify this in the revised version and now also use an easier method (which is used for our new results) to compute the value initialization.

# Questions

> Given the case where both successors are absorbing with zero value, could that provide a way to anchor the values?

We are a bit unsure about your question, but we hope our comment answers it. :)

 Introducing the case distinction from Eq. 20 prevents ill-defined pairings like $\Delta_\theta(s_{random},s_{terminal}) = V(s_{random}) - V(s_{terminal}) = V(s_{random})$, because we are not able to compute a single absolute value. By considering your suggestion $ \Delta_\theta(s_{terminal},s^{\prime}_{terminal}) = 0 $ we cannot see a way of anchoring values. 

> Would it be possible to visualize the value differences between states for a few states or trajectories?

This is a good suggestion. But it will require some additional coding. We will try to include this into a future revision.

> Why does the paper focus on 49 while the usual full set of ATARI games includes 57 games?

Valid question, but there is no real reason for that. Schulman et. al. (PPO) presented their ALE result with (only) 49 games, and so did Pan et. al. (DAE). We just sticked to these games as well.

> In the conclusion, you mention "We hope RV serves as a building block for algorithms that reason natively in the relative domain where decisions are actually made.". What would be the potential advantages given that performance-wise, it does not seem to improve learning?

Fortunately, we were able to improve our results noticeably (please, see our general comment above). In general, we argue that by optimizing for relative values the learning/gradient signal changes significantly. From a function approximation perspective, the potential advantage is that differences might be easier to learn than absolute values. 

> Any setting where this approach might be superior to usual Q-learning based for instance?

Note that we are currently not considering Q-functions. However, this is an interesting direction, but note that the delta Q-function would look somewhat wild:
$\Delta(s, a, s', a') = Q(s,a)- Q(s',a')$. Seems doable, but we have not looked into it, yet.

We thank the reviewer again for their time and hope that the new value initalization clarification and improved results address all concerns.

summary.value: This paper proposes relative value learning, which considers value differences between states instead of the usual absolute values of states. The authors show that value differences satisfy a kind of Bellman operator and inherit the contraction property, which can be utilized to learn value differences in a way similar to classical values (e.g., TD ($\lambda$)). Similar to GAE, the value differences can also be used to construct advantage estimators using TD errors, and the authors prove that such "advantages" are unbiased for policy gradients. Empirical results for the ALE were given, and results show competitive performance compared to GAE and DAE.

strengths.value:
The paper is well-motivated (i.e., the absolute scale is irrelevant in terms of policy improvement), clearly written, and easy to follow.
The theoretical results showing that the value differences satisfy a Bellman equation and can be similarly estimated like classical value functions are quite intriguing, and might open up new ways to design RL algorithms.

weaknesses.value:
While convergence results were given, it is not immediately clear whether learning the relative values actually provides any benefit over traditional absolute value estimators, and empirical results seem to suggest that the two are perhaps not too different in terms of policy optimization.

Regarding the experiments:
1. I would highly suggest reporting aggregated metrics (e.g., median, IQM, or similar) and learning curves alongside per-environment scores. Currently, it's very difficult to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach simply from Table 1 and the description on line 431.
2. It is now well-known that deep RL algorithms often come with high variance, and reporting statistical significance is necessary for comparing the performance of different algorithms [1].
3. The comparison to DAE is not entirely fair, as the reported results [2] use a much larger number of actors (1024 compared to 8), corresponding to significantly fewer PPO iterations.

There are also some interesting details that I think are worth mentioning in the main text, such as how the state pairing is done in practice (line 806). 

[1] Agarwal, Rishabh, et al. "Deep reinforcement learning at the edge of the statistical precipice."  NeurIPS 2021.

[2] Pan, Hsiao-Ru, et al. "Direct advantage estimation." NeurIPS 2022.

questions.value:
1. It looks like relative values can eliminate the shift invariance of the reward functions, and I wonder if there are remaining redundant degrees of freedom that can be fixed. Can the authors elaborate on this?
2. While Section 4 suggests that $B_t$ can increase the variance of the policy gradient estimator and points the reader to Appendix C, this problem is not really addressed in Appendix C either, aside from an empirical demonstration. Can the authors provide a more in-depth analysis on this?
3. Regarding the critic training, can the authors share more details on how the pair sampling affects performance (line 806-809)? Also, it is not clear to me how $\mu$ (Eq 28) affects convergence theoretically. I imagine the $(i, j)$ have to follow a certain distribution that is related to the sampling policy, but this is not really discussed.

# Weaknesses

> While convergence results were given, it is not immediately clear whether learning the relative values actually provides any benefit over traditional absolute value estimators, and empirical results seem to suggest that the two are perhaps not too different in terms of policy optimization.

We fixed a bug and now beat PPO in 61% (previously 47%) of games!! And DAE in 75% (61% before) of games! The aggregated metrics in the revised version (see new Figure 3) also look promising.

Please, see our general comment. 

> I would highly suggest reporting aggregated metrics (e.g., median, IQM, or similar) and learning curves alongside per-environment scores. Currently, it's very difficult to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach simply from Table 1 and the description on line 431.

Thanks for your suggestion. We now show your suggested aggregated metrics (in Figure 3) for PPO, DAE and PPO+RV (ours). Also, the ablation shows now all PPO+RV learning curves (red in updated Figure 4) that are used for Table 1.

Please, also see our general comment.

> It is now well-known that deep RL algorithms often come with high variance, and reporting statistical significance is necessary for comparing the performance of different algorithms [1].

We increased the number of seeds to 10 (previously 5) for each game and report variance.

Please, see our general comment. 

> The comparison to DAE is not entirely fair, as the reported results [2] use a much larger number of actors (1024 compared to 8), corresponding to significantly fewer PPO iterations.

Good point. DAE is doing fewer PPO iterations that are based on **more** data while we are doing more PPO iterations that are based on **less** data. To us, it is not obvious which setting is strictly better. As you may noticed, our paper shows the DAE results from Table 7 in the DAE paper (same network architecture like ours). The authors also experimented with different big network achitectures and noticeably improve the performance (Table 8 & 9 in DAE paper) despite having the same (low) number of PPO iterations. Therefore, we argue that quantity does not necessarily beat quality, so we believe our comparison is useful and fair. Also note that the PPO baseline (large number of iterations) is still not able to beat DAE on some games.

> There are also some interesting details that I think are worth mentioning in the main text, such as how the state pairing is done in practice (line 806). 


Our new ablation (Appendix E) shows that non-uniform state pairing has only a tiny influence. 

Please, also see our general comment. 


# Questions

> It looks like relative values can eliminate the shift invariance [...], and I wonder if there are remaining redundant degrees of freedom that can be fixed. Can the authors elaborate on this?

Yes, absolutely. We are currently working on a fork of relative value learning that directly (and only) learns preferences given a reward function. Like "Is A better than B? Or is B better than A?". That would mean the agent learns only the sign of the difference. We can't say more, but stay tuned ;)

> While Section 4 suggests that $B_t$ can increase the variance of the policy gradient estimator and points the reader to Appendix C, this problem is not really addressed in Appendix C either, aside from an empirical demonstration. Can the authors provide a more in-depth analysis on this?

You are probably refering to Table 2, right? We also put a figure in Appendix C (Figure 5, on the second page), which we thought would clarify the issue in general. 

**Explanation of the figure:** When we could somehow know the (for us unknown) offset $C$ we can directly compute $B_t$ and visualize it for a rollout of length $T$.
Let's look at the brown curve ($C=5$). At the start $B_t$ is almost constant ($\approx 0.8$) and inflates GAE with a constant, but then it falls of. When $t\rightarrow128$, $B_t$ almost vanishes and our R-GAE value is now very close to real GAE. Almost no inflation anymore, therefore there exists a noticeable variance over the rollout, that can be demonstrated for arbitrary $C$.

**Question:** Beyond that, is there anything that you would like to see? We improved the figure explanation text and caption in the revised version. But we are unsure what you would like to see in a new analysis.

> Regarding the critic training, can the authors share more details [...]? Also, it is not clear to me how (Eq 28) affects convergence theoretically. I imagine $(i,j)$ the have to follow a certain distribution that is related to the sampling policy, but this is not really discussed.

Yes, this question puzzled us as well. So, we did an ablation study (Appendix E) on pair sampling. We observed a rather weak influence.

We thank the reviewer again and hope our updates satisfactorily address the concerns! :)

# Questions

> Based on the above, could the authors [...] also report variance in performance on the benchmark?

Please, see our answer above.

**TLDR:** Yes, the variance and other aggregated metrics are now reported!

> Based on the above, could the authors differentiate their contributions from the mentioned prior work [1] [...] ?

Yes, of course. While Dimitri Bertsekas [1] has the intuition in 1997 that relative quantities can be beneficial for learning, he leaves the idea largely unexplored in terms of theory for relative value critics (including bootstrapping), episodic handling, policy-gradient integration and different optimization behavior (R-GAE), DeepRL practice, experiments and ablation. We substantially modernize and scale this idea:

- **Pairwise Bellman Formulation and Targets.** We present in our paper the complete theory necessary for understanding relative value learning. We define a pairwise Bellman operator on antisymmetric functions and show it is a $\gamma$-contraction with unique fixed point. After that we derive 1-step, $n$-step, and $\lambda$-return targets that also correctly handle episodic environments (the four termination cases derived in Appendix A) and show that relative differences are invariant to shifts (see Appendix B). Readers only need our paper to get a complete picture and understanding of relative value learning (not given in [1]). And none of these episodic constructions and targets are present in [1].

- **Connection to Policy Gradient.** We show that generalized advantage estimation (GAE) can be reconstructed from differences alone (R-GAE), and that it results in an unbiased PG estimator up to a constant. We also derived the relationship between GAE and R-GAE precisely. Prior work on cost-to-go differences does not connect relative critics to modern policy-gradient theory.

- **DeepRL.** Our work provides a novel and reproducable DeepRL algorithm. It uses a siamese antisymmetric network architecture, a new trajectory-ranking algorithm for relative value initialization, and an integration with PPO that removes the absolute critic. We demonstrate that this purely relative critic is competitive on 49 Atari games. [1] does not provide any of this. Furthermore, we compare it to related methods and do ablations. 

Based on these facts, we are very confident that our paper is a great contribution for the DRL community.


We hope to convinced you about the novelty of our work and would be happy if you would consider to raise your score. :)

We thank the reviewer for the engagement!

> Regarding Q2, you claim "...It thereby increases the variance of our policy-gradient estimate...". However, there is no analysis suggesting this is the case. Note that the claim here is regarding policy gradient, not just the values.

Ah, yes sorry. We mentioned this a bit hand-wavy in Section 4. However, we discuss your concern now properly and derive the problem analytically in Appendix C (Variance Analysis of the Relative Policy Gradient) with the empirical evidence shown in Figure 4. Please see the new revised version!

**Short version:**
We show that $B_t$ acts as an additional noise term in the second moment of the R-GAE policy gradient estimator ($g_{rel}$): $\mathbb{E}[\|g_{rel}\|^2] \approx \mathbb{E}[\|g_{std}\|^2] + \mathbb{E}[\|\nabla \log \pi\|^2 B_t^2]$. Since $B_t$​ scales with the unknown offset C, a large uncorrected C quadratically increases the variance of the policy gradient! This is why we introduced the ranking algorithm (Section 4) to reduce $B_t$. Then our ablation (Figure 4) validates this importance empirically. 

> Regarding the DAE baseline, if I'm understanding correctly, the original DAE paper also used 40M frames ("Each agent is trained independently for 10 million and 40 million in-game frames for the MinAtar and the ALE environments, respectively."), but with fewer PPO iterations. This may explain why the PPO (w/ GAE) numbers reported in Table 7 might be lower than the ones reported in the present work. For a fair comparison, I would recommend aligning the experimental settings (particularly the number of PPO iterations) with those used in the original DAE work. This would help ensure that any performance differences can be attributed to the method itself rather than to differences in training procedures.

In addition, the DAE authors describe (see DAE paper page 19, Appendix C, C.4.3 PPO Hyperparameters, Link: https://ewrl.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/advantage__ewrl_.pdf) that using 1024 actors is the result of hyperparameter search!

So, if using 1024 actors is the best hyperparameter setting for DAE, is it then fair to enforce this hyperparameter also on PPO (Schulman et. al.) and PPO+RV (ours)? We think that the comparison in the DAE paper (Table 7) against PPO is not entirely fair, since PPO can be tuned to be better than DAE for Atari. To our knowledge, our paper reports the performance of all methods (PPO, PPO+RV and DAE) with their best hyperparameter setting!

Nonetheless, it would be interesting to see, what happens to our method (PPO+RV) if we increase the number of actors to 1024.  Our problem right now is, that our implementationis tuned for speed and low memory profile (we use tensordicts, cudagraphs, and do everything in VRAM to complete runs in 65 minutes) which we only have with small number of actors.
So the "1024" experiment would require a large rewrite of our code, which we are unable to deliver until 02.12. In addition, our "wall-clock time" would probably increase with 1024 actors.

**Experiments:** Not exactly what you are asking for, but we did run DAE with 8 actors (like PPO and PPO+RV), so that DAE has the **same** number of PPO iterations as both other algorithms and report performance.

We thank the reviewer for the feedback, and for the positive comments on clarity and the breadth of the empirical evaluation. However, you rated our soundness only as fair. So, we are curious how we can further improve your assessment.

# Weaknesses

> Limited theoretical novelty. The main theoretical results are direct consequences of standard value-based RL theory. The proposed “pairwise Bellman operator” is simply the subtraction of two standard Bellman equations, and the contraction proof follows immediately from classical results.

Of course, this is not rocket science, but details are important and certainly non-trivial. While DQN (Mnih et. al., 2013) did not invent Q-learning itself, it presents, refines and scales the Q-learning theory to a point, where DQN is considered a substantial contribution by the community. Our paper provides a complete and detailed theoretical and algorithmic picture on relative value learning. You only need our work to find out why relative value learning works, what its properties are and how to actually build it. Despite the equivalence, the relative value function is different from simply post-processing an absolute value function. The function class itself is constrained (antisymmetry, zero diagonal, siamese architecture), eliminating the gauge degree of freedom at the model level rather than at the level of the target or reward shaping. On top of that, considering our new relative value loss and neural networks in general it has implications for function approximation and regularization that are non-trivial and difficult to predict. 

Further, we provide theory on how to properly approximate the pairwise Bellman operator via sampling, which is not given by the literature that deals with standard TD/GAE or absolute values. We systematically derive 1-step, $n$-step and $\lambda$-return targets that operate purely in the pairwise space (see cases 1-4 in Eq. 20 and Appendix A). Other works do not spell out these pairwise terminal cases and they certainly do not  trivially follow from "simply subtracting two standard Bellman equations". Without them relative value learning breaks for episodic tasks such as Atari.

> Similarly, R-GAE and the unbiasedness result are reformulations of known properties of GAE. While the relative formulation is conceptually neat, it doesn’t introduce new theoretical insights.

It is still important to find the exact relationship between R-GAE and GAE as we did with $\tilde A_t = A_t + B_t$, where $B_t$ is a trajectory-constant baseline that depends on the initial value
$C = V^\pi(s_0)$ and decays with $\gamma \lambda$. This decomposition, together with the gauge-invariance lemma in Appendix B, clarifies exactly how the unidentifiable offset of $V^\pi$ manifests inside R-GAE and how it interacts with variance. We also validate the effect of $B_t$
in Table 2 and Figure 5, which (to our knowledge) is a new analysis of a widely-used estimator rather than a simple restatement. It is certainly an important insight. As a consequence, we were able to develop the trajectory ranking algorithm which was not trivial to find. Applying trajectory ranking significantly improves the performance as demonstrated in our ablation (see Figure 4).   

> Marginal empirical contribution. The empirical results show that PPO+RV performs on par with PPO and DAE, but without consistent or significant improvement. This makes it difficult to justify publication at a top-tier venue like ICLR on empirical grounds alone.

By fixing a bug, we improved our result noticeably. PPO+RV beats PPO in 61% of the games (47% before) and DAE in 75% (previously 61%).  In addition, we report standard deviation (Table 1) and aggregated metrics (Figure 3).

Please, see our general comment.

> Insufficient related work discussion. The paper cites relatively few references and overlooks related research on invariance, reward shaping, normalization, and average-reward formulations, which would help clarify where this work fits in the broader context.

What literature are you referring to exactly? Relative value learning is a very general concept, isn't it? What did we miss? The old and revised version already cites potential-based shaping (Ng et al., 1999) and average-reward MDPs (Abounadi et al., 2001; Puterman, 2014, Bertsekas, 2025). What do you mean by Normalization and Invariance?

> Overall, the paper feels more like a conceptual reinterpretation of existing ideas than a substantial theoretical or algorithmic advance.

Okay, but what existing ideas are you referring to? We argue that focusing on the relative distance between states is a substantial departure from the usual way of approaching reinforcement learning.

By learning relative values, there are certainly algorithmic and theory advances needed to get a properly working method. As Figure 4 (Ablation for value init) demonstrates, one needs to consider offset initalization for GAE. Developing this insight was not possible without exactly deriving the relationship between R-GAE and GAE (as in Lemma 3.2). Solving the potential issue that Lemma 3.2 raises is neither trivial nor a "conceptual reinterpretation"! In addition, we consider deriving the 1-step target and its case distinction (see Eq. 20 and Appendix A) as a substantial advance as well.

# Questions

> Since the pairwise Bellman operator is mathematically equivalent to subtracting two standard Bellman updates, what concrete advantage does this formulation bring in practice beyond removing the value offset?

From a function approximation perspective, the potential advantage is that differences might be easier to learn than absolute values. We think this needs to be explored and is not trivial to answer by saying they are equivalent. Also, we improved the performance (see Table 1 and Figure 3) over PPO and DAE.

> How sensitive is the performance of PPO+RV to the way state pairs are sampled?

Interesting question. This question also came to our mind. So, we did an ablation study and found out that it is not very sensitive. For more information, please see our general comment.


> Have you tested RV in continuous-control or off-policy settings, where relative value estimation might interact differently with bootstrapping?

Unfortunetely, not yet. As acknowledged in Limitations, our experiments are currently  conducted on discrete-action Atari with on-policy actor-critic.

We hope we were able to adress your concerns and would appreciate if you reconsider your score. :) Also, we are happy to continue this discussion here. :)

summary.value: Relative Value Learning (RV) replaces traditional absolute state-value estimation with a framework for learning pairwise, antisymmetric differences $\Delta(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. This approach targets the relative quantities that actually drive decision-making while eliminating arbitrary value offsets. The authors provide a rigorous theoretical foundation by defining a pairwise Bellman operator, proving its $\gamma$-contraction, and deriving Relative Generalized Advantage Estimation (R-GAE) for unbiased policy gradients. To maintain stability at scale, the method incorporates a trajectory ranking algorithm and specific case handling for terminal states. Experiments across the Atari-49 benchmark show that this relative critic outperforms PPO in 61% of games and DAE in 75%, establishing it as a theoretically sound and empirically effective alternative to absolute value critics.

reviewer_concerns.value: The authors successfully addressed the primary empirical concerns by identifying a bug in the relative value initialization, leading to updated results where the proposed method outperforms the PPO baseline in sixty-one percent of games. They also resolved requests for statistical rigor by increasing the evaluation to ten seeds and providing aggregated metrics like IQM. The novelty critique regarding a previous submission from Bertsekas (1997), was mitigated by demonstrating that the earlier work lacked the operational details, terminal state handling, and trajectory ranking necessary for deep reinforcement learning. Technical questions about estimator stability were answered through a newly derived variance analysis in the appendix. Remaining concerns are limited to a minor disagreement over the fairness of the DAE baseline comparison, specifically regarding the alignment of PPO iterations, which the authors addressed by arguing for the inclusion of hyperparameter selection in the evaluation. Reviewer 5Wrj also maintained a conceptual objection that the framework is a mathematical reformulation of existing equations, though the empirical success and detailed implementation derivations provided during the rebuttal largely invalidate the claim that the contribution is marginal.

reviewer_scores.value: Reviewer 8vTK and Reviewer K8y5 both provided initial ratings of 6. Since the authors implemented the specific requests for increased seeds and aggregated metrics that Reviewer 8vTK highlighted, the score for that reviewer likely would have remained a 6 or increased to a 8. Reviewer K8y5 participated in the discussion but maintained reservations regarding the alignment of the DAE baseline comparison and the policy gradient variance analysis, suggesting that the rating would have stayed a 6. Reviewer YGuv gave a 4 based on marginal performance and a quite old citation. Because the rebuttal corrected a bug that led to a significant performance lead over PPO and addressed the citation specifically, this reviewer likely would have moved to a 6. Reviewer 5Wrj provided a 2 and did not respond to the rebuttal. While the improved Atari results weakened the argument that the contribution was marginal, the fundamental objection regarding the simplicity of the theoretical operator suggests this reviewer would not have moved beyond a 4.

Dear Area Chair,

given the paper reassignment, we would like to give a summary about our contribution and how the rebuttal adresses the reviewers' concerns. We appreciate your effort in this unusual situation!

---

### 1. Contribution and Scope

At a high level, our method proposes a new way of doing reinforcement learning. We look at value estimation from a relative point of view in order to directly obtain quantities that actually drive decision making. The points below outline its core contribution and scope:

- The method learns *directly value differences* instead of absolute values, removing the arbitrary value offset and matching what actually matters for control (action preferences depend only on differences).
- It introduces a *pairwise Bellman operator* with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, plus well-posed 1-step / n-step / $\lambda$-targets.
- It reconstructs *advantage estimation* entirely from pairwise terms (R-GAE) and introduces a trajecory ranking algorithm to reduce policy gradient estimator variance.
- When dropped into PPO as a critic, the approach is *competitive across 49 Atari games*, showing that relative critics are a viable alternative to standard absolute value critics.

---

### 2. Two Reviewers Recommend Acceptance
**Reviewer 8vTK** and **Reviewer K8y5** recommend acceptance (both rating 6) and find the motivation, theory, clarity and contribution compelling. All of their concerns are directly adressed in the revised version or with rebuttal comments.

- We implemented the improvements they requested: added **aggregated metrics and variance**, increased to **10 seeds**, simplified **relative value initialization**, expanded **ablations** (state-pair sampling, trajectory ranking), and derived **estimator variance**.
- Updated results show **substantial empirical improvement** (PPO+RV(ours) > PPO on 61% of games; > DAE on 75%), resolving the earlier concern that performance gains were only marginal.

---

### 3. Clarifying Misunderstandings Raised in the Two Rejecting Reviews

**Reviewer YGuv** (rating 4) provides a **very short** review:
- It focuses on only a small subset of the paper. **All the weaknesses** like variance reporting, empirical strength, and the distinction from prior work were raised in **only two sentences**, without engaging with many of the technical sections (e.g., the pairwise targets, R-GAE derivations, trajectory ranking algorithm, variance analysis). However, we adress all concerns in the revised version.
- The novelty critique is based on a **single reference from 1997** that contains **only a conceptual remark**, not an operational and scalable method like ours. The reviewer does not discuss the new theoretical and algorithmic components developed in our paper.
- The empirical concern (“does not improve over PPO”) **was accurate** for the initial version but is **no longer correct** after the bug fix and revised value initialization method.

**Reviewer 5Wrj** (rating 2):

- The reviewer states that entire research areas were “overlooked” but **does not cite any specific papers**, while we already cite reward shaping and average-reward MDP references (which is criticized as missing related work).

- The empirical assessment (“no improvement over PPO”) is **based on the initial submission**. The revised results show clearly **improved performance** (61% over PPO, 75% over DAE, see Table 1 and Figure 3)

- Several of the reviewer’s central claims appear to rest on **misunderstandings** of the paper. The core claim is that the theory is “just subtracting two Bellman equations”, but this **overlooks many technical contributions**. These do not simply follow from classical TD theory (e.g. the full derivation of 1-step/n-step/λ targets with four terminal cases, the R-GAE relation and decomposition, the estimator variance analysis, and the trajectory-ranking solution needed for stability on Atari).

- The reviewer characterizes the theoretical contribution as “not novel”, yet **does not engage** with major parts of the paper where novelty is evident (e.g. like handling of episodic environments, the construction of well-posed targets, the policy-gradient connection + variance analysis, and the trajectory ranking algorithm).

- Overall, the review seems unusually negative relative to both the paper’s content and the other reviewers’ assessments (see **Contribution: (good, good, fair)** and **Soundness: (excellent, good, fair)**).

Thank you again for your time and consideration!

We thank all the reviewers for their helpful feedback and improved the paper accordingly. The changes since the original submission are summarized below.


**(1) Optimal Value-Offset Estimation.** In Sec. 4.1 we replaced the previous value offset heuristic by a simpler and better method. The new one corresponds to using the row-wise mean as the natural least-squares offset estimator given noisy pairwise differences. Due to the changes, Figure 2 has been updated.

 **(2) Small Bug Fix.** 
We identified a small implementation bug. When a rollout contained multiple episodes, only the first episode in that rollout received the correct relative value initialization. This is now fixed (everyone gets the correct value init) and Figure 4 has been updated. 

**(3) New Atari Results.** The Atari results in Table 1 have been recomputed because of (1) and (2). With these corrections, our proposed method PPO+RV improves substantially. It now exceeds PPO on 30 / 49 games (61%) and DAE on 37 / 49 games (75%) [old version: 23 / 49 (47%) and 30 / 49 (61%)]. Several environments show notable gains (e.g., Q*bert, Video Pinball, Atlantis, Time Pilot, Up’N Down). 

**(4) Statistical Precipice.** For better statistical significance, our new results now average over 10 (instead of 5) seeds for each game. We also added standard deviations for all presented algorithms and report additional aggregated metrics like Median/IQM etc. as suggested by reviewer K8y5. [Pan et. al. (DAE) kindly provided us their original data to compute the standard deviation for Table 1 and aggregated metrics for Figure 3.]

**(5) Appendix.** We improved the explanation for Figure 5.

**(6) Ablations.** We now show all 49 games in the value initalization ablation (Figure 4) to visualize the learning curves of our method (red) that are used to compute the values in Table 1. Furthermore we did ablate on the state pair sampling as recommended by multiple reviewers. Our results show that different state pair sampling (uniform, 33% biased, 66% biased) has only a tiny impact on performance, so we decided to put it in only as a small chapter in Appendix E.

Please, have a look at our revised version!

summary.value: This paper introduces Relative Value Learning (RV), a reinforcement learning framework that focuses on learning pairwise value differences $\Delta(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$ instead of absolute value functions. The authors derive a “pairwise Bellman operator,” show that it is a γ-contraction, and propose a relative version of Generalized Advantage Estimation (R-GAE). They integrate RV with PPO and evaluate the approach on Atari games, reporting comparable or slightly improved performance in some cases.

strengths.value:
- The paper is clearly written and well organized
- The empirical results are conducted on a reasonably broad benchmark

weaknesses.value:
- Limited theoretical novelty. The main theoretical results are direct consequences of standard value-based RL theory. The proposed “pairwise Bellman operator” is simply the subtraction of two standard Bellman equations, and the contraction proof follows immediately from classical results. Similarly, R-GAE and the unbiasedness result are reformulations of known properties of GAE. While the relative formulation is conceptually neat, it doesn’t introduce new theoretical insights.
- Marginal empirical contribution. The empirical results show that PPO+RV performs on par with PPO and DAE, but without consistent or significant improvement. This makes it difficult to justify publication at a top-tier venue like ICLR on empirical grounds alone.
- Insufficient related work discussion. The paper cites relatively few references and overlooks related research on invariance, reward shaping, normalization, and average-reward formulations, which would help clarify where this work fits in the broader context.
- Overall, the paper feels more like a conceptual reinterpretation of existing ideas than a substantial theoretical or algorithmic advance.

questions.value:
1. Since the pairwise Bellman operator is mathematically equivalent to subtracting two standard Bellman updates, what concrete advantage does this formulation bring in practice beyond removing the value offset?
2. How sensitive is the performance of PPO+RV to the way state pairs are sampled?
3. Have you tested RV in continuous-control or off-policy settings, where relative value estimation might interact differently with bootstrapping?

summary.value: The paper proposes learning relative value differences compared to directly predicting state value. They integrate the proposed idea of relative value learning with PPO and evaluate its performance on the Atari benchmark.

strengths.value:
- The idea of estimating relative values is well motivated and might additionally have benefits under function approximation settings (as noted in \[1\])  
- The paper is well written and the details of the method and experimental setup are clearly outlined.

weaknesses.value:
- The idea of using cost-to-go differences or relative value was explored earlier in \[1\], so perhaps the idea of estimating value difference is not necessarily novel. However, its application in DeepRL might be novel.  
- The proposed approach does not necessarily improve over the PPO baseline in the evaluated benchmark, it would be good to also indicate the observed variance in scores to suitably contrast against the baselines.

questions.value:
- Based on the above, could the authors differentiate their contributions from the mentioned prior work \[1\] and also report variance in performance on the benchmark?
